Shunem
SHOO-nem
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Shunem, a town of Issachar in the Jezreel valley; the home of the hospitable woman who lodged Elisha and whose son he raised from the dead.

📖 Biblical Definition

Shunem was a town of Issachar in the valley of Jezreel, remembered chiefly for the great-hearted woman whose story fills 2 Kings 4. Perceiving that Elisha was a holy man of God who passed her way, she and her husband built and furnished a little chamber on the wall, that the prophet might lodge there. For her kindness Elisha promised, against all hope, that she would bear a son, and so it came to pass. When the boy, grown, died suddenly of a stroke in the harvest field, she laid him on the prophet's bed, rode hard to Carmel, clung to Elisha's feet, and would not be turned aside; the prophet came, prayed, stretched himself upon the child, and God restored him to life (2 Kings 4:8-37). Years later Elisha's word saved her from famine and recovered her land (2 Kings 8:1-6). Shunem was also where the Philistines encamped before the battle of Gilboa (1 Sam 28:4), and the home of Abishag, who cherished the aged David (1 Kings 1:3). Shunem stands in the dictionary as the town of the Shunammite woman, a lasting picture of hospitality to God's servants and of faith that holds fast to God in the face of death, rewarded by the God who gives and restores life.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A town of Issachar in the Jezreel valley (2 Kings 4), home of the hospitable Shunammite woman who lodged Elisha; God gave her a son and, when he died, raised him through the prophet — a picture of hospitality and persevering faith.

SHUNEM, proper noun. A town of Issachar in the valley of Jezreel.

Home of the woman who built a chamber to lodge Elisha (2 Kings 4:8-10).

Where God gave her a son in reward for her kindness.

Where, when the child died, Elisha raised him to life (2 Kings 4:32-37).

Also the camp of the Philistines before Gilboa (1 Sam 28:4) and home of Abishag (1 Kings 1:3).

📖 Key Scripture

2 Kings 4:9 — "And she said unto her husband, Behold now, I perceive that this is an holy man of God, which passeth by us continually."

2 Kings 4:10 — "Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick: and it shall be, when he cometh to us, that he shall turn in thither."

2 Kings 4:26 — "Run now, I pray thee, to meet her, and say unto her, Is it well with thee? is it well with thy husband? is it well with the child? And she answered, It is well."

2 Kings 4:34 — "And he went up, and lay upon the child, and put his mouth upon his mouth, and his eyes upon his eyes, and his hands upon his hands: and he stretched himself upon the child; and the flesh of the child waxed warm."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Shunem needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the honor of hospitality to God's servants and the persevering faith that says "It is well" in the face of death, answered by the God who restores life.

expand to see more

Hospitality-diminished misreading. A transactional age sees little value in opening one's home to a passing servant of God. The Shunammite built a room for the prophet expecting nothing, and God rewarded her beyond her asking. The dictionary holds the biblical honor of hospitality: to receive a prophet in the name of a prophet is to receive a prophet's reward (Matt 10:41), and kindness to God's servants is kindness the LORD Himself remembers and repays.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faith that holds fast in grief. When her son lay dead, the Shunammite did not despair but rode straight to the man of God, and to every anxious question answered, "It is well." The dictionary commends her persevering trust: faith in the hour of loss does not deny the pain but clings to the God of life, and Shunem became the place where the God who gives also proved Himself the God who raises the dead.
